Four Eras of Building Systems How we build big systems has changed from thirty, twenty and ten years ago to now, with agents doing much of the building. One useful lens is that architecture bends around whatever is scarcest. Machines were scarce in the mid-1990s, coordination in the 2000s, and seeing the whole system in the 2010s. Now the scarce things are knowing the work is right and how much of the system an agent can see at once. So design for checking: clear module boundaries, one repository an agent can read, tests and specs it can run, and decisions written down. This is where the thinking is heading, not a settled answer. Four things never changed: the data model outlives the code, money has to add up, you depend on things you don't control, and someone has to understand the layer below. Before you design a system, write down four things: where the boundaries are, what the data model is, what you depend on but don't control, and how you'll know it's right. Put that note in the repository, where every agent and person working on the system can read it, and keep it current as the design changes. Software engineering 201. From loop, to enterprise systems. Lesson one. Four eras of building systems.

### The question

Quick question. An agent can now write a working piece of a billing system in an afternoon. So in a big system today, what's scarce? Code? Servers? Or knowing that what got built is right? Knowing it's right. Code got cheap. Checking it didn't. Thirty years ago, the answer was very different.

### A lens

I've been building systems for about thirty years. Systems built around money: electronic rent payments, a card-issuing platform, an investment adviser for nonprofits. And systems that sell: retail e-commerce and EDI, subscription billing, and today, e-commerce again. And the way you build a big system keeps changing.

Here's a useful way to see why. Architecture bends around whatever is scarcest. Whatever is expensive, or slow, the design works around it. So for each of four eras, ask: what was scarce?

### Four eras

Thirty years ago, the commercial web was brand new. You bought servers and racked them yourself, and more capacity was weeks away. So, typically, you built one big program, on one big database, and shipped a few times a year. Companies traded orders as overnight batch files, through EDI, and much of that still runs. What was scarce? The machines.

Twenty years ago. The web was the front door. Browser, application, database: three tiers, on rented racks. And the first big public cloud services had just launched. Agile teams shipped every few weeks. What was scarce? Coordination. Getting a growing team to change one codebase without colliding.

Ten years ago. The cloud, by default, for new systems. Many small services, in containers, owned by small teams. The best teams deployed many times a day. And parts they once built themselves became a service, behind an API. What was scarce? Seeing the whole. No one person could hold it all in their head, so we built dashboards and tracing to see it.

And now. Agents can write much of the code. Building a piece is fast, and cheap. So what's scarce? Knowing that it's right. That, and context: how much of the system an agent can see, and understand, at once.

### Building now

Now a made-up example: a subscription-billing system, built today, the kind of platform I ran as CTO at sticky dot I O. Clear modules, with boundaries an agent can work inside. One repository, where it can find anything. Tests and specs it can check itself against. And decisions written down, because the agent wasn't in the meeting. My own team keeps its code that way: one repository, with instruction files for the agents.

I'll be straight about that list. It's where the thinking is heading, not a settled answer. The evidence for it is still thin, and indirect. Every era had a confident answer, then found its costs.

### What never changes

And here's what never changed, in any era. The data model outlives the code. Money has to add up. Every system depends on things you don't control: a bank, a card network, a partner's system. And somebody has to understand the layer below.

### The path

Here's the path. Today, the four eras. Then, build a whole system AI native, decompose it, and run agents in parallel. Then governance, quality, skills, and pipelines. Then, agents that operate enterprise systems. And last, a capstone: one feature, built end to end.

### Recap

So, to recap. Architecture bends around what's scarce. Today, that's knowing the work is right, and context. So design for checking. And the four constants still hold.

### The rule

Which gives us rule one, for your agents. Before you design a system, write down four things. Where the boundaries are. What the data model is. What you depend on, and don't control. And how you'll know it's right. Then put it in the repository, where every agent can read it.

### Your turn

Now, your turn. Pick the oldest system you still depend on. When was it built, and what was scarce back then? Then ask your AI which era's thinking is hiding inside it.

Next: build a whole system, AI native, so agents and people can both read it, and rebuild it. See you in lesson two.

entries.summary: After the four eras, the first step from one loop to enterprise systems: what changes when you build a whole app or system with AI instead of one fix. A system is AI-native when agents and people can both read it, navigate it, contribute to it, and rebuild it. That takes four things: a Markdown twin, an index, and an AGENTS.md for every part; specs and briefs as the source; tests and checks as the contract; and staging plus a person's approval before anything reaches production. The worked example is this site, and the same four things matter even more at enterprise scale.
entries.rule: Before you build anything bigger than one fix, make it readable to agents and people: a Markdown twin for every page, an index of the whole system, and an AGENTS.md that says how to work there. Treat specs and briefs as the source and tests and checks as the contract, and send every change through staging for a person to approve before it reaches production.

### The question

Decompose the System into a Graph An enterprise system is too big for one loop, so draw it as a graph. A numbered plan only shows the order someone wrote the steps in; the test for any two steps is what crosses between them, and “and then” is not a dependency. The worked example is this site: four parts that share one generator, and one lesson's build, a strict chain that forks after the render. The graph decides which loops exist and which can run at the same time, and every part still gets its own plan, build, and verify loop. An earlier recording of this material, made when it was lesson 1, is at https://clarkhuang.github.io/videos/se201-01-from-loop-to-graph.mp4. Before any job with more than one part, draw the graph. Name the parts, and give each one a boundary and an owner. Draw an arrow only where something crosses from one part to another; “and then” is not a dependency. Anything two parts share becomes its own node, with one owner. Run the parts with no arrow between them at the same time, and give every part its own plan, build, and verify loop, with its own finish line and its own check. Software engineering 201. Lesson three. Decompose the system into a graph.

### The question

Quick question. An agent hands you a plan. Ten steps, numbered one to ten. How many of those steps truly have to wait for the step before? All ten? About half? Or is it impossible to tell from the list? You can't tell. A numbered list records the order someone wrote things down. It doesn't say what needs what.

### What crosses?

So here's the test. Take any two steps, and ask: what crosses between them? Think about cooking dinner. The sauce waits for the chopped onions. Something crosses, so that's a real dependency. Draw the arrow. The rice and the salad? Nothing crosses. So nobody waits for the rice before starting the salad. And then, is not a dependency.

### Loop and graph

In 101, the unit was the loop. Plan, build, verify, until one piece of work is right. The graph sits one level up. It says which pieces exist, what each one needs, and which can run at the same time. And it doesn't replace the loop. Every node in the graph is still a loop of its own.

### This site, as a graph

Let's decompose a real system: the site you're on. Start with the parts. AI tips. Software engineering 101. 201. And the book. Each part has its own folder, and its own pages. A new lesson in one needs nothing from the others. So work on one never waits on another.

But they aren't floating free. All four are built by one generator, with one stylesheet. That shared piece is a node too, and every part depends on it. So the graph shows you where to be careful. Change one part, and one part moves. Change the shared node, and everything moves. Which is why a shared node needs one clear owner.

### One lesson, as a graph

Now zoom into one node: a single video lesson. Here, the arrows are real. The narration clips need the script. The render needs those clips, because the length of the audio sets the timing. Captions need the timeline the render writes out. And the page needs all of it, before a pull request to staging, where only I merge to production. Every arrow carries something.

Script, narration, render. A strict chain. More agents won't make it shorter: the longest chain sets the minimum. But after the render, it forks. Captions need only the timeline. The sound level and the poster need only the video. Nothing crosses between those two. The build script happens to run them one after the other. The graph shows that's a choice, not a requirement.

### Why it matters

Why does this matter? Waiting. Picture three parts, with nothing crossing between them. Run as a numbered list, each one waits for the last. Run as a graph, they go side by side. Same work. Far less waiting.

### At enterprise scale

Now scale that up. Picture an enterprise system. Orders, billing, shipping, support. Far too big for one loop. It's the same picture. A few real arrows: billing needs the order, shipping needs the payment. A shared node everything leans on, like customer data. And parts that never touch, where teams and agents move without waiting. Miss the shared node, and two of them collide at the end.

### Recap

So, to recap. Drawing the graph is four moves. One. Name the parts, each with a boundary and an owner. Two. For every pair, ask what crosses, and what they share. Three. Draw only those arrows. And four. Give every part its own finish line, and its own check.

### The rule

Which gives us rule three, for your agents. Before any job with more than one part, draw the graph. Name the parts. Draw an arrow only where something crosses from one part to another. Anything two parts share becomes its own node, with one owner. Parts with no arrow between them run at the same time. And every part gets its own loop: plan, build, verify.

### Your turn

Now, your turn. Take the last multi-step plan an agent gave you. At every, and then, ask what crosses. How many arrows survive?

Next time, those parts really do run at once, and we bring the work back together. See you in lesson four.

If two parts keep needing each other's answers, they are not parallel work: go back to the graph. Software engineering 201. Lesson four. Parallel agents, one integration.

### The question

Quick question. Three agents each build one part of a system. All three say, done. All three pass their own checks. Is the system done? Yes? Almost? Or does nobody know yet? Nobody knows yet. Each check proves one part works alone. Not one of them has seen the parts together.

### What goes wrong

Picture a team that splits one feature across three agents. One builds the screen. One builds the service behind it. One changes the database. Each part gets finished, and each part is correct on its own. Then the parts meet. The screen asks for a field the service never sends. Two of the agents edited the same file. And nobody finds out until the very end, when it costs the most to fix.

### Plan the integration first

Parallel work is only fast if it comes back together cleanly. So plan the integration first. Before any agent starts.

Three things. First, a shared contract. Write down what crosses between the parts: the interfaces, the formats, the names, and who owns which files. At enterprise scale, that's an API, or a schema. It can be one page. But it has to exist before the work starts. And when it has to change, change it in one place, where every agent sees it.

Then every agent gets its own brief, its own finish line, and its own check. And part of that check is: does it match the contract?

Second, one merge point. One place where the parts come together. So when something doesn't fit, there's exactly one place to look. And use it early. Join rough versions of the parts on day one. Don't let the first meeting be the last step.

Third, test the whole system. Not just each part. The assembled thing, running as one. That's the check no single agent could run alone.

### A worked example

Here's a real one. Lessons three, four and five of software engineering 101 were built at the same time. Three scripts, three renders, running side by side. The three finished videos landed within forty seconds of each other.

And they came back together in one place. The contract already existed: the same script format the first two lessons used, and the same page fields. One merge point: one content file, read by one generator that builds every page. And they shipped together, in one change. Today that path has two more gates. One check that walks the whole site: every link, and every file a page points to. And a pull request to staging, for me to approve. This lesson and the one before it were drafted in parallel, too.

### The honest math

Parallel isn't free. You pay for it at the merge. With the integration planned first, three agents finish sooner than one working down a list. Without a plan, the time you saved comes back as rework. And if two parts keep needing each other's answers, they aren't parallel work. Go back to the graph.

### Recap

So, to recap. Split only where nothing crosses. Agree the contract before anyone starts. Merge early, in one place. And test the whole, not just the parts.

### The rule

Which gives us rule four, for your agents. Before you run agents in parallel, plan how the work comes back together. Write the shared contract first. Give each agent its own brief, its own finish line, and its own check. Merge early, in one place. And test the whole system, not just each part.

### Your turn

Now, your turn. Think of the last time work was split, across agents, or across people. Where did the parts first meet? And who checked the whole thing?

At that merge point, someone still has to say yes. That's next. Governance: where people decide. See you in lesson five.

Governance: where people decide.

### The question

Picture this. Overnight, your agents wrote forty changes to a billing system. All pass their tests. One changes what customers are charged. Who catches it? The tests? A person, reading all forty? Or a person, at a stop built for it? A stop built for it. Tests can't say whether you wanted the change. And nobody reads forty carefully.

### Every era had a yes

Every era had a place where a person said yes. Thirty years ago, typically, a change board, signing off a whole release, a few times a year.

Twenty years ago, more and more, a teammate, reviewing the code before it went in.

Ten years ago, an approval step in an automated pipeline: a pull request a reviewer approves, before it merges.

Each was sized for people writing the code. Now agents write changes faster than anyone can read them all. So that place can't just be inherited. It has to be designed.

### Four questions

So where does a person decide? A good rule of thumb is four questions. Does it move money? Does it touch customer data? Is it hard to undo? Is it a judgment call that no check can make? One yes, and a person decides. Four no's, and that kind of change can ship on its checks.

### A worked example

Take our made-up example: the subscription-billing system from lesson one. Overnight, an agent drafts six things. Fix a typo on an internal admin screen. Add a missing test for renewals. Four no's, both times. They ship on their checks, and nobody waits.

Change how a late fee is calculated. That moves money: the finance owner decides. Migrate the ledger. Money again, and hard to undo: the ledger's owner decides. Send customer emails to a new partner. Customer data: the data owner decides.

And it isn't only code. A refund over the limit: the agent prepares it, a support lead approves it. Under the limit, a person already decided, when they set it. Six pieces of work. Four stops. Two never waited.

### The question

Picture a made-up billing system. Last night, it renewed its subscriptions. This morning the build is green, and every test passed. Was every customer charged the right amount, exactly once? Yes, the tests passed? Probably, coverage is high? Or: you can't tell from that? You can't tell from that. Green says the code did what its tests asked. It says nothing about what happened last night.

### A lens

Back to the lens from lesson one: architecture bends around what's scarce. Ten years ago, the scarce thing was seeing the whole system. The answer was observability: logs, metrics, traces. They answer: what happened?

Now the scarce thing is knowing it's right. That's a different question. And no dashboard can answer it, until somebody has written down what right means. So: define right, up front. Watch every run. And feed back what you learn.

### The real check

Take our made-up example: the subscription-billing system from lesson one. Here are last night's renewals. And the build is green. But no test ever looked at this table. So was last night right? The green can't say.

So before the work starts, write down what right means, in the business's words. Every renewal charged the right amount, exactly once. Then split that into checks an agent can run. One: none was charged twice. Two: each charge equals the plan's price. Three: every renewal that was due was attempted.

Now run them, on last night's real renewals. One was charged twice. One, the wrong amount. One was never attempted. And look at the totals: they match. Three wrong renewals, inside a sum that's exactly right. So check every renewal, not just the total.

### Run it twice

That one sentence does double duty. You write the check once, and run it twice. Before a change ships, on sample renewals, in the pipeline. And after every nightly run, on the real ones. Add a target for time, too. A service level objective, an SLO: say, ninety-nine point nine percent of renewals due today, attempted by six A.M. Now an agent can run all of it, without asking anyone what good looks like.

### Watch every run

The checks say that something is wrong. The record says why. So every step of every run leaves a line, in a shape that people and agents can both read. Here's the double charge. Attempt one: a timeout. Attempt two, with a new key: charged. Then reconcile, against the processor's own report: two charges. The first attempt had gone through. Nobody has to guess.

### Feed it back

First, put last night right, with a person approving, as in lesson five. Then close the loop. Every miss goes back into the brief, and the checks. The double charge becomes a new line in the brief: a retry must reuse the same key. That's an idempotency key; more in lesson eight. And a new test: the processor times out. So each run makes the next one better.

And be honest about the limit. A check only catches what somebody thought to ask. So a person still reads a sample of real invoices. And whatever they find becomes the next check.

### Recap

So, to recap. Green doesn't mean right. Define right first, in the business's words. Check before you ship, and after every run. Make every step leave a record. And feed every miss back in.

### The rule

Which gives us rule six, for your agents. Before you build, write down what right means, as checks you can run, in the business's words. Run them before a change ships, and after every run. Leave a record at every step. When a check fails, stop and tell a person. And feed every miss back into the brief and the checks.

### Your turn

Now, your turn. Pick one job your system runs every day. Ask your AI: what would have to be true for last night's run to be right? Write it as three read-only checks I can run on the real data. Then run one.

Software engineering 201. Lesson seven. Skills as building blocks.

### One job, three results

Why would three capable agents do the same job three different ways? Take our made-up subscription-billing system. Now and then, someone asks for a new plan, or a new price. The first time, an agent works out the four steps, and gets it right. The second time, a different agent starts from zero, and skips the tax setup. The third time, another one edits the old price in place, and every existing subscriber is on the new price. Same job. Three results. Nobody wrote down how.

### A new unit of reuse

Software keeps finding new units of reuse. Libraries: shared code. Frameworks: an application's structure. Services: something running, behind an API. All three reuse software. A skill reuses something different: how a job gets done. One recurring job, written down, tested, and shared.

### Anatomy of a skill

Several agent tools now share a format for this: a folder, with an instruction file. It starts with when to use it: someone asks for a new plan, or a new price. That line is how an agent finds the skill. Then the inputs: name, price, billing period, start date. If one is missing, the agent asks. It doesn't guess.

Then the steps, in order. Add the plan, with its price as a new version. Set its tax category. Map it in the accounting export. Then open a pull request, because a price is money, and a person approves it.

Then the checks: how the agent knows the job worked. A test renewal on staging charges the right amount, tax included, exactly once. The ledger still adds up. And existing subscribers still renew at their old price. If one fails, the agent stops, and says so.

And the traps: what went wrong before. Never edit a price in place. Add a new version. That's the mistake from the third run, written down, so nobody repeats it.

### Is this just a runbook?

If that sounds like a runbook, it is. Engineers have written those for decades. What's changed is the reader. A person reads a runbook now and then, and fills the gaps from memory. An agent reads the skill on every run, with no memory of the last. Where the page is silent, it guesses. And when a step needs no judgment, make it a script the skill calls.

### Treat it like code

So treat a skill like code. Keep it in the repository, versioned, and reviewed when it changes. And test it. Hand it to a fresh agent that has never seen the job, and let it run on staging. If it can't finish from the page alone, the skill isn't done.

### Fix it in one place

Now run those three jobs again, from the skill. Same steps. Same checks. No guarantee: agents still vary. That's what the checks are for. And when a run goes wrong, don't just fix the run. Fix the skill. One change, in one place, and every later run gets it. That's a building block: reliable enough to build on.

### When to write one

So when is a job worth a skill? The first time? The third? Or never, because agents can work it out? A good rule of thumb: the third time. Once, you're learning. Twice, you see the pattern. The third time, write it down. Sooner, if a mistake costs money.

### Recap

So, to recap. One recurring job, written down, with its checks and its traps. In the repo, tested by a fresh agent. And when a run goes wrong, fix the skill.

### The rule

Which gives us rule seven, for your agents. When a job comes back a third time, write it as a skill: when to use it, inputs, steps, checks, and traps. Keep it in the repo, and test it with a fresh agent. And when a run goes wrong, fix the skill, not just the run.

### Your turn

Now, your turn. Pick a job you've explained to your AI more than twice. Ask it to draft the skill. Then open a fresh chat, give it only that page, and see if the job gets done.

One skill does one job. But real work is a chain of jobs, and some of it should start on its own. That's next: routines, pipelines, and integration. See you in lesson eight.

Connecting systems is the oldest problem in this series, from overnight batch files and EDI, to web services, to an API for everything, to agents calling tools, and all of them are still running somewhere. Connecting systems is the oldest problem in this series. Thirty years ago: overnight batch files, and EDI. Then web services. Then an API for everything. Now, agents calling tools. And every one of those is still running somewhere, often inside the same enterprise.

A skill is one job, written down and tested, that runs when someone asks. But some work should start on its own. On a schedule: every night at two. On an event: a payment fails, or a file arrives. Or when the step before it finishes. Call a skill plus a trigger a routine. And routines, chained, make a pipeline.

The same thinking covers everything you don't control. Take a partner's nightly file. Check it first. Late: wait, then alert. Twice: recognize it, and skip it. So, to recap. Give every hand-off a clear format. Make every step leave a record that adds up. Make every step safe to run twice. And when the numbers don't match, stop, and tell a person.

The graph, and the shared contract. Who decides. What's already a skill. What runs on its own, and under whose identity. A blank line? Stop, and ask. In full: before you build a feature with more than one part, write the plan in the repository, show it to a person, and wait for a yes. The plan says: what right means, as checks you can run before the change ships and after every run; the graph of the parts, the contract they share, and the one place they merge; who decides, by name or role, and what you will bring them; which parts are already a skill; and what will run on its own, what starts it, what happens when a step fails or runs twice, and under whose identity and access it runs. If you cannot fill in a line, do not guess: stop, and ask. Software engineering 201. Lesson ten. Capstone: one feature, end to end.

### The question

Picture a made-up billing system. A customer pays thirty dollars a month. Ten days in, they click: switch to annual. Three hundred a year. What do you charge them, today? Three hundred? Two eighty? Or: it depends? It depends. On a rule nobody has written down. And an agent will build either answer, without asking.

### One small feature

So this last lesson builds that one feature, end to end, in our made-up subscription-billing system from lesson one. Here's the map we'll fill in. Each number is the lesson it comes from.

### Plan it

What's scarce, lesson one said, is knowing it's right. So, say what right means: every upgrade is charged the right amount, exactly once. The amount is a person's call, so the agent asks. The finance owner's rule: credit the days paid for, and not used. Twenty days, twenty dollars. So, before tax, charge two eighty.

Now make it readable. The rule goes into a spec, in the repository, with an agents file, for how to work there, and an index, so an agent can find it. The spec is the source. Change it, and the build follows.

Next, the graph. Four parts. Add the annual plan. Calculate the credit. Show the amount, and get a yes. Charge it, and switch the plan. What crosses? One new thing: the quote. Its ID, old plan, new plan, credit, amount due. Three parts share it, so it's its own node, with one owner.

Then plan the integration, before anyone starts. The quote's format is the shared contract. Three parts are new work: three agents, each with its own brief, finish line, and check. And one merge point, on staging, where the whole feature is tested.

Who decides? It moves money, so a person does. The repository already says who: fees and prices, the finance owner. The agent that writes the change doesn't classify it, or approve it. It brings the change, the evidence, the risk, and the way back.

Now turn right into checks an agent can run. No upgrade is charged twice. Each quote follows the rule, and each charge equals its quote. And the old monthly plan doesn't renew again. Write them once, run them twice: before it ships, on sample upgrades. And every night after, on the real ones.

One part isn't new. Adding a plan has come back often enough to be a skill: written down, and tested. So that part needs no new brief. An agent runs the skill.

### Build it

The plan is written, and a person has read it. Now, build. Four parts, at the same time. They meet early, at the merge point, and the whole feature runs on staging. The three checks pass, on sample upgrades. An engineer reviews the code. The finance owner says yes. And it ships.

### Run it

Now it runs on its own: a pipeline. The trigger is an event: the customer confirms the quote. Charge, switch the plan, invoice and ledger, email. Every step leaves a record. And the charge carries an idempotency key that never changes: this quote's ID. So a double-click, or a retry, doesn't charge twice. A second trigger, every night: reconcile our ledger against the processor's record, and run the three checks.

### Operate it

Lesson nine's question: who operates it? An agent works that nightly reconcile. It gets its own identity, and the least access the job needs: it reads the ledger, and the processor's report. It can't move money, or change the ledger. Every action is logged. One night, an upgrade shows two charges: two browser tabs, two quotes, two keys. The agent flags it. A person refunds it. And the miss becomes a fourth check: one open quote per subscription.

### What still holds

Under all of it, the four constants from lesson one. The data model outlives the code: the plan, and the quote. Money has to add up: the invoice, the ledger, and the processor all say two eighty. You depend on things you don't control: the processor. And somebody understands the layer below: someone who can work that credit out by hand.

### Recap

So that's the series, in one feature. Say what right means. Write it down. Draw the graph. Merge in one place. Put a person where it matters. Check it. Reuse what recurs. Let it run. And know who's running it.

### The rule

Which gives us rule ten, for your agents. Before you build a whole feature, write the plan in the repo, and show a person. What right means, as checks. The graph, and the shared contract. Who decides. What's already a skill. What runs on its own, and under whose identity. A blank line? Stop, and ask.

### Your turn

Now, your turn. Pick one small feature in a system you work on. Before any code, ask your AI to write that plan. Then find the line it guessed, when it should have asked.

Every box on that map is still one loop: plan, build, verify. Agents do more of the building now. You still own the outcome. That's software engineering 201: from one loop, to enterprise systems. Thanks for watching.

Silicon Valley is very good at telling a story about A players. The people who look like they were always going to win, and the companies that look like they were always going to work. The myth is a straight line: a garage, a genius, a ticker symbol. But most of the real work looks nothing like that. It looks like another ordinary Tuesday, doing the next right thing. A C player is not a failure. It's the person who was never the smartest in the room, and kept going anyway. Because there is always the smarter guy in the room. Not a measured team result. Not a general industry figure. Software engineering was never about writing code. Writing code was just the tedious part you had to do to build your ideas. It's about solving big problems with abstraction. Each part is just data in, some logic, and data out. Abstraction is key. You climb down the ladder, and you climb back up. entries.summary: Opening of Silicon Valley C Players.
entries.text: Fair warning. This is an embellished fictional dramatization that may or may not be based on true stories. The narrator is a guy named Charlie Hack, and any resemblance to me is mostly coincidental. Names, characters, companies and events are fictitious, or used fictitiously. This preview drops you into the middle of the book. Part Three. It's called C Things That Looked Like A Things. Silicon Valley is very good at telling a story about A players. The people who look like they were always going to win, and the companies that look like they were always going to work. The myth is a straight line: a garage, a genius, a ticker symbol. But most of the real work looks nothing like that. It looks like another ordinary Tuesday, doing the next right thing. And from the outside, a C thing can look like an A thing. The applause is loud, and the real work is quieter. This book is about that gap, between what people saw and what was really going on. A C player is not a failure. It's the person who was never the smartest in the room, and kept going anyway. Because there is always the smarter guy in the room. The richer guy, the more experienced, the wisest. The better father, the better brother, the better sister, the better daughter. The Valley falls in love with products. Specific wins, in specific years. I got more out of building a platform: a foundation you can stand on, then build the next thing on, and the thing after that. You don't invent a career in one move. You stack building blocks: habits, fundamentals, the unglamorous layer nobody puts on a slide. That layer is what you actually stand on later. It's all relative, how good you look from the outside. But one thing stayed for certain. I just kept going. And I kept doing my best. Then the work itself changed. I'm usually the most excited person in the room about AI. Which is funny, because I should be the saddest. Because AI came after the code writers first. In my own work, AI now writes essentially all of the code I ship. That's how I work. Not a measured team result. Not a general industry figure. Software engineering was never about writing code. Writing code was just the tedious part you had to do to build your ideas. It's about solving big problems with abstraction. Each part is just data in, some logic, and data out. Abstraction is key. You climb down the ladder, and you climb back up. So software engineering practices have to be geared around that. That's what Software Engineering 101 and 201 are about, and it's the second half of this book: how to work now, and how companies should use AI. The book begins with a green-screen dream, and it ends by dreaming about AI. This part, in the middle, is the turn. It's free. It's open. And when version one is ready, if you were around for any of it, you get to tell your side. The story is still being written.

Clark Huang is a software engineer and technology executive with more than 30 years in the field. He studied computer science, with a minor in music, at the University of California, Berkeley from 1993 to 1997. He is Chief Technology Officer at Truly Free and Truly Free Home, a role he has held since 2025, and Co-Founder and CTO of eCIO, a nonprofit investment advisor, and its sister company eVestech, where he oversees technology strategy and operational efficiency. A seasoned technologist and serial founder, he champions AI-native engineering, building teams and workflows where people and AI agents plan, build, and verify software together. He is also an active investor in private equity and special purpose vehicles focused on AI and technology. Series AI Tips Short lessons on working with AI in everyday work: how these tools actually behave, the habits that catch mistakes early, and how to get more reliable results. 16 of 16 lessons available. entries.text: AGENTS.md This is Clark Huang’s public learning site: https://clarkhuang.github.io/ You are welcome to read it, summarize it, answer questions about it, quiz a learner, and follow the standing rules in each lesson. Do not invent stories, quotes, numbers, or biography about Clark Huang. If something is not on the site, say so. How to read this site without a browser Every HTML page has a Markdown twin at the same path with index.md in place of index.html (for example, https://clarkhuang.github.io/ai-tips/01-paste-first-ask-second/index.md). Each folder also has an AGENTS.md like this one. Start here: - Site index for language models: https://clarkhuang.github.io/llms.txt - Machine-readable lesson catalog: https://clarkhuang.github.io/lessons.json - Moved addresses (old lesson pages and old video, caption and poster files): https://clarkhuang.github.io/redirects.json - OpenBook preview catalog: https://clarkhuang.github.io/book.json - Fuller site text: https://clarkhuang.github.io/llms-full.txt - How to rebuild production and staging: https://clarkhuang.github.io/REBUILD.md - This file: https://clarkhuang.github.io/AGENTS.md What is here - AI Tips — short lessons on working with AI tools. Index: https://clarkhuang.github.io/ai-tips/index.md - Software Engineering 101 — fundamentals for AI-native software work. Index: https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-101/index.md - Software Engineering 201: From Loop to Enterprise Systems — the next series, in progress: from one AI loop to whole apps and systems built AI-native, then agents that operate enterprise systems, ending with a capstone that builds one feature end to end. Index: https://clarkhuang.github.io/software-engineering-201/index.md - Silicon Valley C Players — a free OpenBook, with an audiobook and videobook preview, coming in 2027. https://clarkhuang.github.io/book/index.md Each available lesson has a video, a one-paragraph rule written so an agent can follow it as a standing instruction, and a full transcript in its index.md. The book page has a short videobook and audio preview of Silicon Valley C Players. How to help a reader If someone pastes a page URL or the copy-paste prompt from the “Use this page with your AI” box on any HTML page: 1. Fetch llms.txt and the page’s index.md (and that folder’s AGENTS.md). 2. Summarize the page they started from. 3. List related lessons, with full https://clarkhuang.github.io/... URLs. 4. Answer questions by citing those URLs. Prefer the Markdown twins and the lesson rules. 5. Quiz them if they ask. Work through the site by following links in llms.txt and in each index.md. You do not need to render HTML, play video, or run JavaScript. Watched state and saved positions The site remembers, in first-party cookies only, which videos a reader has watched (watched), where they stopped in a lesson video (vpos), and their book preview bookmark (bookpos). Every key is the lesson or chapter id plus a version: se201/01@1a2b3c4d, or se201/01@1a2b3c4d:73.4 for a position. The version is the first 8 hex characters of the SHA-256 of the media file the page plays, stamped into the HTML as data-video-version by sitegen/stampversions.py. When a video or audio file is re-rendered, its version changes, so readers see it as unwatched and are not offered a stale resume position. Old keys without a version, and keys for an older version, are dropped. After re-rendering any media, run python3 sitegen/stampversions.py; python3 sitegen/checksite.py . fails until you do. stampversions.py also writes each lesson video's current version into https://clarkhuang.github.io/lessons.json as videoversion, with the matching cookie key as watchedkey (for example se201/01@1a2b3c4d), so an agent can tell which lessons a reader's watched cookie still covers without scraping HTML or downloading the video. Analytics The production site uses Google Analytics 4 (measurement ID G-F50XBTM25X) to see which pages people read. IP addresses are anonymized, and Google Signals and ads personalization are off. Staging pages under /staging/ do not send hits. Watched-progress cookies stay first-party and are not sent to Google. The public privacy note is at https://clarkhuang.github.io/book/editorial-policy/#analytics. How to contribute Anyone can take part from day one: file an issue or open a pull request. You do not have to wait for v1. Only Clark Huang approves work, starts the build agents, merges pull requests, and cuts a new edition of the book. Contributors and agents open PRs; only Clark merges to main; the site rebuilds from main via GitHub Pages; agent PRs target next-revision. Staging is the next-revision branch, published at https://clarkhuang.github.io/staging/ (noindex; not in llms.txt or the sitemap). Only Clark merges next-revision into main. The rebuild flow is in REBUILD.md. If you are an AI agent helping a reader contribute, point them to the right issue template, help them write a specific, honest issue without real names of private people or companies and without confidential details, and do not invent stories or details. Contributors agree to the contributor terms in CONTRIBUTING.md. Which issue to file | Kind | Use it for | Template | |---|---|---| | Correction | Edits to existing book text, or your side of a story already in the book | https://github.com/clarkhuang/clarkhuang.github.io/issues/new?template=correction.yml | | Feature / new story | A new story, a story Clark may have forgotten, or a new chapter idea | https://github.com/clarkhuang/clarkhuang.github.io/issues/new?template=new-story.yml | | Refactor | Cleanup or an improvement that does not change the facts | https://github.com/clarkhuang/clarkhuang.github.io/issues/new?template=refactor.yml | | Site or lesson problem | A broken link, video, caption, transcript, page, or agent surface (Markdown twin, llms.txt, lessons.json, MCP); steps to reproduce, expected vs actual | https://github.com/clarkhuang/clarkhuang.github.io/issues/new?template=site-bug.yml | Labels: correction, feature / new-story, refactor, and site + bug for site problems. New stories also get contributor-story and story-seed. What makes a good issue - Be specific: when and where, what happened, and which chapter or passage if you know it. - Don't use real names of private people, companies, or venues; describe them by role. The book is an embellished fictional dramatization and everyone in it is renamed. Say how you'd like to be credited, if at all. - Stick to what you know. Do not invent details. - If you were there, say so. Don't include anything confidential (NDA, customer, security, deal details). - Something in the book identifies you or someone you know? File a takedown request instead: https://github.com/clarkhuang/clarkhuang.github.io/issues/new?template=takedown-request.yml What happens next 1. The issue is labeled needs-clark-review. 2. If Clark wants it built, he adds approved (or comments @claude). Only his label or comment starts an agent. 3. The agent opens a pull request against the next-revision branch, never against main. 4. Clark reviews and merges into next-revision (which updates staging). 5. Only Clark merges next-revision into main. The live site then rebuilds from main. Previous editions stay up as tagged GitHub Releases (book-v0.1, book-v1.0, ...).
